overview.title: Inspecting the dataset and the commonsense baseline

summary:
The sentence from p.382 ends: because samples are shuffled, consecutive sequences in a batch (such as `samples[0]` and `samples[1]`) are not necessarily close in time.

**Listing 13.8** takes one batch from `train_dataset` and prints `samples shape: (256, 120, 14)` and `targets shape: (256,)`. That is 256 windows of 120 hourly steps with 14 features, plus 256 target temperatures.

**13.2.2 A commonsense, non-machine-learning baseline.** Before trying black-box deep learning models, try a simple commonsense approach. It is a **sanity check** and sets a **baseline you must beat** to show that more advanced models are useful. Such baselines help especially on new problems without a known solution. The classic example is an **imbalanced classification** task: with 90% class A and 10% class B, always predicting "A" gives 90% accuracy, so any learning-based model must beat 90%. Elementary baselines can be surprisingly hard to beat.

For the temperature series, two assumptions are safe: it is **continuous** (tomorrow's temperatures are likely close to today's) and **periodic with a daily period**. The commonsense prediction is therefore: *the temperature 24 hours from now equals the temperature right now*. It is evaluated with the **mean absolute error (MAE)**, `np.mean(np.abs(preds - targets))`, i.e. $\frac{1}{n}\sum_i |\hat{y}_i - y_i|$, in degrees Celsius.

**Listing 13.9** begins `evaluate_naive_method(dataset)`. It initializes a running sum of absolute errors (`total_abs_err = 0.0`) and a counter (`samples_seen = 0`), then loops over the dataset's `(samples, targets)` batches. The rest of the listing, on p.384, takes the last timestep's temperature feature of each sample, un-normalizes it with `std[1]` and `mean[1]`, accumulates the errors and returns their average. The results (2.44 degC validation, 2.62 degC test) are on p.384.

paragraphs.excerpt: consecutive sequences in a batch (like samples[0] and samples[1]) aren’t necessarily temporally close.
paragraphs.what_it_says: End of the sentence from p.382: because of shuffling, consecutive sequences in a batch, like samples[0] and samples[1], are not necessarily close in time.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The batch index carries no temporal meaning. Each row is an independent five-day window drawn from anywhere in the split's time range.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Models must not assume any relation between rows of a batch. Stateful tricks that carry state from one batch row to the next would be wrong here.

paragraphs.excerpt: Before you start using black box, deep learning models to solve the temperature
paragraphs.what_it_says: Before using black-box deep learning models, try a simple commonsense approach. It acts as a sanity check and sets a baseline that more advanced models must beat. This helps on new problems without known solutions. For example, in an imbalanced classification task with 90% class A and 10% class B, always predicting A is 90% accurate, so a learning-based approach must beat 90%. Such baselines can be surprisingly hard to beat.
paragraphs.what_it_means: A metric value means nothing in isolation. The baseline converts 'my model has X error' into 'my model is Y% better than doing the obvious thing'. It also checks the pipeline: if a trained network can't beat the trivial rule, either the data/labels are broken or the model isn't learning anything useful.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This sets up the chapter's storyline. The dense model (p.384) and the 1D convnet (p.386) struggle to beat the baseline, and only the recurrent models do so clearly (for example 2.27 degC validation MAE with a dropout-regularized LSTM, p.398, a 7% improvement).
paragraphs.technical_idea: For imbalanced classification, the majority-class baseline accuracy equals the frequency of the most common class. Beyond the book: this is why precision/recall or balanced accuracy are often reported alongside plain accuracy.

A test that catches gross errors in the data or pipeline.

paragraphs.excerpt: In this case, the temperature timeseries can safely be assumed to be continuous
paragraphs.what_it_says: The temperature series can be assumed continuous (tomorrow's temperatures are likely close to today's) and periodic with a daily period. So the commonsense approach is to always predict that the temperature 24 hours from now equals the current temperature, evaluated with the MAE metric, defined as np.mean(np.abs(preds - targets)).
paragraphs.what_it_means: Continuity says the temperature can't jump arbitrarily. A daily period says that 24 hours later we are at the same point of the day-night cycle, so the daily component of the temperature cancels out. What remains is the day-to-day weather change, which is exactly what makes forecasting hard. MAE averages the absolute errors, so it is in degC and easy to interpret.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Because the forecast horizon (24 hours) equals the daily period, this is a 'seasonal naive' forecast and is especially strong. A naive forecast for a 12-hour horizon would be much worse, because it would compare night with day.
paragraphs.technical_idea: In terms of the dataset: prediction = temperature at the last input hour (row N + 714), target = temperature at row N + 858, exactly 144 rows (24 h) later. The baseline's MAE is therefore the average absolute 24-hour temperature change.

terminology.meaning: Varying smoothly over time, without large sudden jumps.
Average of |prediction - target|, in the target's units.
Beyond the book: predicting the value from one period earlier.

concepts.name: Commonsense (non-learning) baseline
concepts.definition: A trivial, hand-specified prediction rule used as a reference score and sanity check before training models.
concepts.intuition: If your expensive model can't beat a coin flip or 'same as yesterday', something is wrong.
concepts.technical: Classification: always predict the majority class (accuracy = its frequency). Forecasting: predict the value one period earlier; here, the current temperature for 24 hours later.
concepts.significance: All chapter-13 models are judged against the 2.44 degC validation MAE of this baseline (p.384).
concepts.example: 90% class A: always predicting A gives 90% accuracy.
concepts.misconception: A model with good-looking metrics is automatically useful. It must beat the baseline.

concepts.name: Mean absolute error (MAE)
concepts.definition: The average absolute difference between predictions and targets.
concepts.intuition: On average, how many degrees off are we?
concepts.significance: The chapter's evaluation metric. Being in degC makes results easy to interpret.
concepts.example: Errors of 1, -3 and 2 degrees give MAE = (1 + 3 + 2)/3 = 2 degC.
concepts.misconception: MAE and MSE rank models identically. MSE penalizes large errors more, so the two can disagree.

concepts.name: Imbalanced classification
concepts.definition: Classification where class frequencies differ greatly.
concepts.intuition: Rare-event detection: most of the time nothing happens.
concepts.technical: The majority-class predictor reaches an accuracy equal to the majority class's frequency, without learning anything.
concepts.significance: Shows why raw accuracy can be misleading and why baselines matter.
concepts.example: 90% A / 10% B gives a 90% accuracy baseline.
concepts.misconception: 90% accuracy is always good. It may be exactly the trivial baseline.

concepts.name: Periodicity
concepts.definition: Regular repetition of a pattern over time.
concepts.intuition: Same time tomorrow looks a lot like now.
concepts.technical: A 24-hour horizon equals the daily period, so the naive forecast cancels the daily cycle.
concepts.significance: Justifies the 'temperature in 24 h = temperature now' baseline.
concepts.misconception: Periodicity alone makes forecasts exact. Weather variation still causes about 2.4 degC average error.

math.title: Mean absolute error

variables.meaning: True target temperature for sample i (targets), in degC

math.operations: Elementwise difference, absolute value, then mean.
math.purpose: Measures the average forecast error, in the same units as the target.
math.interpretation: An MAE of 2.44 means the prediction is off by 2.44 degC on average (p.384).
math.intuition: Signed errors would cancel out; the absolute value counts over- and under-predictions equally.

math.title: The commonsense forecast
math.source_text: always predict that the temperature 24 hours from now will be equal to the temperature right now

variables.meaning: Row of the last hourly input step of window N (6 x 119)

math.operations: Copy the last observed temperature forward by 24 hours.
math.interpretation: The baseline MAE is the mean absolute 24-hour temperature change over the split.
math.intuition: Same time tomorrow will be like now.
math.numerical_example: If it is 4.0 degC at the end of the window and 6.5 degC 24 hours later, the baseline error for that sample is 2.5 degC, about the average reported on p.384.

math.title: Majority-class baseline accuracy
math.source_text: If your dataset contains 90% instances of class A and 10% instances of class B ... Such a classifier is 90% accurate overall

variables.meaning: Frequency of class c in the data

math.operations: Pick the most frequent class and predict it always.
math.purpose: The minimum accuracy a learned classifier must exceed.
math.interpretation: With 90/10 classes, 90% accuracy reflects no skill at all.
math.intuition: Bet on the favourite every time.

code.title: MAE definition
code.what_it_does: Computes the mean absolute error between arrays of predictions and targets.

line_explanations.explanation: Elementwise subtraction, absolute value, then mean over all elements.

code.title: Computing the commonsense baseline MAE (first part)
code.what_it_does: Begins a function that computes the baseline MAE over a whole dataset by accumulating absolute errors batch by batch. The loop body and the calls are on p.384.

line_explanations.explanation: Takes any of the three datasets (the book calls it on val_dataset and test_dataset, p.384).
Running sum of absolute errors and running count of samples, so the final mean is exact even though the last batch is smaller.
Loops over batches. On p.384 the body computes preds = samples[:, -1, 1] * std[1] + mean[1], the un-normalized temperature at the last input hour, and adds np.sum(np.abs(preds - targets)).

code.inputs_outputs: Input: a dataset of (samples, targets). Output (after the p.384 lines): the average absolute error in degC.
code.algorithm: Streaming mean: sum of errors divided by the number of samples.
code.theory_link: Implements the 'temperature in 24 hours = temperature now' rule evaluated with MAE.
pitfalls: Averaging per-batch MAEs instead of summing errors would slightly overweight the smaller last batch; the sum-and-count approach avoids this.
The input temperature is normalized (Listing 13.6) but the targets are in degC, so the prediction has to be un-normalized with std[1] and mean[1] (p.384). Forgetting this gives a meaningless MAE.

deeper.title: Why this baseline is strong
deeper.body:
Break the temperature into a slow seasonal part, a daily cycle and weather fluctuations. Predicting the value exactly 24 hours later from the current one:

- cancels the **daily cycle** (same phase of the day),
- leaves an error of only about 1/365 of the **seasonal** swing, which is tiny,
- leaves the **24-hour weather change** as the whole error.

A model can only beat the baseline by predicting weather changes from pressure, humidity, wind and so on. That is a much harder signal, which explains the modest gains reported later (7% for the best LSTM, p.398).

deeper.title: Analogy: the 'same as yesterday' forecaster
deeper.body: A shop that orders tomorrow's bread by copying today's sales will be right most days. A fancy demand-forecasting system is only worth buying if it beats that habit, especially on the days when something changes. The book's baseline is that habit applied to temperature.

deeper.title: Other baselines worth trying (not in the book)
deeper.body:
- **Persistence of the mean**: predict the average temperature of the five-day window. This is usually worse, because it ignores the most recent state.
- **Climatology**: predict the historical average temperature for that day of the year and hour. This captures seasonality but ignores current weather.
- **Blend**: average persistence and climatology. Often slightly better than either.

The book uses the simplest persistence rule, which is enough to set a meaningful bar.

misconceptions.claim: A baseline is only needed when the model performs badly.
misconceptions.correction: The book recommends establishing it before any modeling, as a sanity check and a bar to beat.

misconceptions.claim: 90% accuracy on a 90/10 imbalanced problem shows the classifier learned something.
misconceptions.correction: Always predicting the majority class already gives 90%.

misconceptions.claim: The naive forecast works only because temperature changes slowly.
misconceptions.correction: It also relies on the daily period: a 24-hour horizon compares the same time of day, cancelling the daily cycle.

misconceptions.claim: Consecutive rows of a batch are consecutive in time.
misconceptions.correction: The samples are shuffled; samples[0] and samples[1] need not be close in time.

takeaways: Batches are (256, 120, 14) inputs and (256,) targets, and rows are not temporally ordered.
Always establish a commonsense, non-learning baseline first: it is a sanity check and the bar to beat.
On imbalanced classification, the majority-class rule's accuracy (for example 90%) is the bar.
Jena baseline: the temperature 24 hours from now equals the temperature now, justified by continuity and the daily period.
Evaluation metric: MAE = np.mean(np.abs(preds - targets)), in degC.
Listing 13.9 accumulates absolute errors and sample counts over batches; it continues on p.384.

questions.question: A dataset has 95% class A and 5% class B. What accuracy does the commonsense baseline reach?
questions.explanation: Always predicting the majority class A is correct 95% of the time, as in the book's 90/10 example. 50% would be random guessing on balanced classes, and 5% is always predicting B.

questions.question: What two properties of the temperature series justify the 'temperature in 24 h = temperature now' baseline?
questions.answer: It is continuous (tomorrow's temperatures are likely close to today's) and periodic with a daily period.
questions.explanation: These are stated directly in the second paragraph of 13.2.2.

questions.question: Compute the MAE for preds = [10, 12, 8, 15] and targets = [11, 9, 8, 13].
Why does Listing 13.9 sum absolute errors and count samples instead of averaging per-batch MAEs?
questions.answer: Batches can differ in size (the last one is smaller). Summing all errors and dividing by the total count gives the exact mean over all samples.
questions.explanation: total_abs_err and samples_seen are initialized on this page and divided at the end on p.384.

questions.question: What does Listing 13.8 print for targets.shape?
questions.explanation: One scalar temperature per sample in the batch. (256, 1) would need an extra axis, and (256, 120) or (120,) would mean one target per timestep.

questions.question: Would the 'same as now' baseline be as good for a 12-hour horizon? Why or why not?
questions.answer: No. 12 hours later the series is at the opposite phase of the daily cycle (day vs night), so the daily swing adds to the error. The 24-hour horizon matches the daily period, which cancels that swing.
questions.explanation: This follows from the daily periodicity the book invokes to justify the baseline.

questions.question: For a problem you work on, can you name the commonsense baseline and its expected score before training anything?
questions.answer: Open-ended: for example, the majority class, the last value, the same value one period ago, or the training-set mean.
questions.explanation: Applies the book's advice that baselines are especially useful on new problems.
